metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Caron v. United States

Opinion filed: 1998-06-22

Docket No.: 97-6270

Citations:
• 141 L. Ed. 2d 303
• 118 S. Ct. 2007
• 524 U.S. 308
• 1998 U.S. LEXIS 4028

Case holding summaries:
• generally holding that civil rights are understood to include the right to vote, the right to sit on a jury, and the right to seek and hold office
• "The rule of lenity is not invoked by a grammatical possibility. It does not apply if the ambiguous reading relied on is an implausible reading of the congressional purpose."
• upholding Caron’s conviction for being a felon in possession of a firearm, even though his firearm possession was legal under Massachusetts law
• affirming federal firearms convictions where defendant had not regained all firearm rights, even though the weapons he possessed were not proscribed by Massachusetts state fel- ony firearm laws
• convicted felon may not possess rifles or shotguns under § 922(g)(1) despite the fact that such possession was permitted to him 6 No. 04-4022 by state law
• "The rule of lenity is not invoked by a grammatical possibility. It does not apply if the ambiguous reading relied on is an implausible reading of the congressional purpose."
• rejecting application of rule where the “ambiguous” read ing “is an implausible reading of the congressional purpose”
• examining scope of section 921(a)(20) unless clause when state restricted possession of handguns only
• agreeing with appellate consensus that restoration by operation of law has the same legal effect as restoration by act of personal clemency
• "Nothing in the text of § 921(a)(20) requires a case-by-case decision to restore civil rights to this particular offender."
• “Restoration of the right to vote, the right to hold office, and the right to sit on a jury turns on so many complexities and nuances that state law is the most convenient source for the definition.”
• the rule is "not invoked by a grammatical possibility"
• concluding that if state law places any restrictions on a defendant’s ability to possess a firearm, then his previous conviction falls within the definition of 18 U.S.C.A. § 921(a)(20
• rule does not apply "if the ambiguous reading relied on is an implausible reading of congressional purpose"
• firearm identification card can be obtained as a "matter of right"
• requiring use of traditional tools of statutory construction to resolve ambiguities before resorting to the rule of lenity
• courts’ analysis of state law restrictions on the defendant’s firearms rights occurred after the defendant demonstrated a restoration of his civil rights
• explaining that, "[a]s to the possession of weapons,... the Federal Government has an interest in a single, national, protective policy, broader than that required by state law"
• stating that, although Massachusetts state law allows a convicted felon to have rifles after relief from firearm disabilities, Massachusetts does not permit petitioner to have handguns and, therefore, there has been no relief from federal firearms disabilities
• convicted felon may not possess rifles or shotguns under § 922(g)(1) despite the fact that such possession was permitted to him by state law
